chapters.title: Chapter 7: Extreme Value Theory for Tail Risk

children.text: Chapter 3 defined Expected Shortfall as the average loss across the worst slice of outcomes beyond VaR. The GPD fitted across the last two lessons makes that computable in closed form, no averaging over sorted historical data required, just a direct formula built from the same shape and scale parameters already estimated.

body.caption: The closed-form EVT-based Expected Shortfall, derived directly from the GPD's mean-excess property. Valid for xi less than 1, which covers essentially every case encountered in practice.

body.label: EVT-Based Expected Shortfall
body.value: A direct algebraic extension of the GPD-fitted VaR from the last lesson, using the same xi, beta, and threshold u
body.context: No separate model or additional data collection needed beyond what Peaks-Over-Threshold already produced.

children.text: Worked Example: Full EVT VaR and ES Table

body.caption: VaR and ES from the fitted GPD (xi = 0.0355, beta = 0.5207, u = 2.0%)

body.text: ES exceeds VaR at every confidence level, exactly as Chapter 3's coherence requirement demands, and the gap between them narrows slightly in percentage-point terms at higher confidence, mirroring the pattern from Chapter 3's normal-distribution comparison, even though the underlying distribution here is a genuinely fat-tailed GPD rather than a normal curve.

children.text: Closing the Loop: Applying EVT to the Course's Running Position

Apply this fitted GPD to the same Rs 50,00,000 Nifty futures position used since Chapter 2's Parametric VaR lesson, and compare against the normal-distribution figures computed there and in Chapter 3.

body.text: This is the course closing its own loop. Chapter 1 showed Nifty returns have fat tails that a normal distribution understates. Chapter 2 built VaR under a normal assumption anyway, for speed and tractability. Chapter 3 built Expected Shortfall the same way. Now, using a method built specifically to model the tail correctly, both figures come back materially higher, 16.4% and 19.8% respectively, than the normal-distribution methods this exact position has been using throughout the course. Chapter 1's warning was not theoretical, it was quantifiably true of the position this course has been tracking the whole time.

children.text: When to Reach for EVT in Practice

body.title: When Simpler Methods Are Enough vs When EVT Earns Its Complexity

columns.label: Simpler Methods Are Enough
points: Routine daily risk monitoring at 95% or 99% confidence, where Parametric VaR is fast and adequate
Options and nonlinear books, where Monte Carlo's full revaluation matters more than the tail's exact shape
Historical Simulation, when the sample is large enough for the confidence level in question

columns.label: EVT Earns Its Complexity
points: Regulatory capital at 99.9% or beyond, where Basel's FRTB-style requirements demand genuine tail accuracy
Any confidence level where Historical Simulation would need a fraction of an observed exceedance, as Chapter 2 first flagged
Reverse stress testing and genuinely extreme scenario work, where the question is specifically how bad the tail can get

body.title: Compute ES from a Given VaR
body.prompt: A GPD fit gives xi = 0.10, beta = 0.80, u = 3.0%, and a 99.5% VaR of 5.2%. Using the formula ES = VaR/(1-xi) + (beta - xi x u)/(1-xi), what is the corresponding ES, as a percentage?
body.explanation: VaR/(1-xi) = 5.2/0.9 = 5.778. (beta - xi x u)/(1-xi) = (0.80 - 0.10 x 3.0)/0.9 = (0.80-0.30)/0.9 = 0.50/0.9 = 0.556. Summing gives 5.778 + 0.556 = 6.33%, meaningfully above the 5.2% VaR, as expected under a genuinely fat-tailed GPD.

body.title: Deciding Whether EVT Is Worth Building
body.scenario: A small prop trading desk runs a straightforward book of liquid Nifty and Bank Nifty futures, monitored daily at 95% and 99% VaR for internal position limits, with no regulatory capital requirement and no options exposure.
body.prompt: Does this desk need to build an EVT-based VaR and ES framework? What would change your answer?
body.modelAnswer: For routine daily monitoring at 95% and 99% confidence on a liquid, linear futures book, Parametric VaR, cross-checked periodically against Historical Simulation, is likely sufficient, EVT's added rigor mainly pays off at more extreme confidence levels or when the consequences of understating tail risk are severe, such as regulatory capital or reverse stress testing. This would change if the desk faced a 99.9%-or-higher regulatory capital requirement, added meaningful options exposure with real gamma risk, or wanted to size a genuinely rare tail event for capital-at-risk purposes, any of which would justify the extra complexity EVT requires.

body.text: Every method in this course was a different answer to the same question this course opened with: how much can I actually lose? Simpler methods answer it well enough for routine use. Extreme Value Theory answers it specifically where the cost of being wrong is highest, and confirms, with real numbers, that the shortcut assumptions taken early in this course were shortcuts, not the truth.

points: EVT-based Expected Shortfall extends the GPD-fitted VaR from the last lesson with a direct closed-form formula, no additional data or separate model required.

Applied to this course's running Rs 50,00,000 Nifty position, EVT-based VaR99 and ES99 came in 16.4% and 19.8% higher than the normal-distribution figures computed in Chapters 2 and 3, a quantified confirmation of Chapter 1's original fat-tails warning.

EVT is worth its added complexity specifically at extreme confidence levels, for regulatory capital requirements, and for genuinely tail-focused work like reverse stress testing, not for routine daily monitoring where simpler methods remain adequate.

This closes the course: Chapter 1 established why volatility alone cannot measure risk, Chapters 2 and 3 built VaR and Expected Shortfall and made them coherent and verified, Chapter 4 covered what those methods cannot see, genuine crisis scenarios, Chapter 5 decomposed risk across a portfolio, Chapter 6 priced the cost of actually exiting a position, and Chapter 7 closed the loop on the fat-tails problem this course opened with, using tools built specifically for the part of the distribution that matters most.

No single method in this course replaces the others. A complete risk framework runs several of them together, on a schedule, with governance that escalates when they disagree, exactly as Chapter 4's framework lesson described.
